name: Uttara Kanda
title: Uttara Kanda: Sita, Lava and Kusha, and the Ramayana’s Ending
description: Read Uttara Kanda through Ravana’s earlier history, Hanuman’s childhood, Sita’s exile, Lava and Kusha and Rama’s departure, with source and edition notes.
dek: After the coronation, the received epic returns to older histories and opens new wounds. The king who has come home must face obligations that will divide his household again.
summary: Uttara Kanda is the seventh book of the received Valmiki Ramayana. It recounts earlier histories of Ravana and Hanuman, then continues Rama’s reign through Sita’s exile, the birth and recitation of Lava and Kusha, Sita’s return to the Earth, and the departures of Lakshmana and Rama.
editionNote: Narrative references follow the main chapter numbering 1–111 in Hari Prasad Shastri’s translation, available on Wisdom Library. That presentation also inserts supplementary chapters labelled 23b–23f, 37b–37f and 59b–59d. These are noted separately below; 111 is not the total number of entries on its contents page. Critical Edition numbering is different.

sections.heading: How to read the seventh book’s place in the epic
paragraphs: Uttara Kanda belongs to the received seven-book Valmiki Ramayana and is included in the Baroda Critical Edition. Its place in devotional practice and in literary history should be explained without confusing the two. A text can be part of a received tradition while containing material composed at different periods.

The introduction to Robert P. Goldman and Sally J. Sutherland Goldman’s scholarly translation discusses evidence that substantial parts of Uttara Kanda are later than much of the central five books. Similar questions concern portions of Bala Kanda. The point is relative textual development, not a simple verdict that every line of an entire book is either original or false.

This guide therefore includes Uttara Kanda and identifies it whenever its events are being used to explain an earlier part of the narrative. The [Princeton translation’s introduction](https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctt1gsmwj0) offers a route into the scholarship; the chapter references for the narrative below follow Shastri, not that edition.

sections.heading: Why the book returns to Ravana’s past
paragraphs: The sages visit Rama after his victory. Questions about the defeated warriors open a long account of their ancestry and earlier actions. Pulastya, Vishravas and the family of the rakshasas place Ravana within a history much older than the abduction of Sita.

The stories trace the growth of rakshasa power, conflicts with Vishnu, the births and austerities of Ravana and his brothers, and the acquisition of protections that shape their later conduct. Kubera’s relationship with Lanka and Ravana’s seizure of power and wealth explain features of the city first encountered during the war.

Ravana’s encounter with Shiva at Kailasa belongs to this earlier history. The account supplies a context for his name and for a combination that later devotional portraits often emphasize: remarkable power and religious aspiration existing alongside destructive conduct.

sections.heading: Conquest, resistance and the consequences of coercion
paragraphs: Ravana’s travels bring him into conflict with rulers, gods and powerful beings. The stories of Vedavati and Rambha confront his coercive treatment of women and the curses associated with it. These episodes complicate any attempt to turn learning or devotion into an excuse for his actions.

The sequence includes Anaranya, Yama, the sons of Varuna and the conflict in which Ravana’s son gains the name Indrajit. Other encounters show that Ravana’s power is not unlimited: Kartavirya Arjuna captures him, and Vali subjects him to a humiliating demonstration of strength.

The supplementary chapters placed after 23 in Shastri’s presentation add further encounters, including Bali, solar and lunar regions and the Maha-Purusha. Their lettered numbering should be retained when citing them. They should not be silently folded into a differently numbered edition.

sections.heading: Hanuman’s childhood explains an earlier silence
paragraphs: Agastya tells Rama about Hanuman’s childhood. The account includes the attempt to reach the sun, Indra’s blow, Vayu’s withdrawal and the gifts by which the gods respond. Hanuman’s power is extraordinary before he ever joins the mission to find Sita.

The following chapter explains the curse of the ascetics after his youthful disruptions of their hermitages. The condition concerns his awareness of his strength and its renewal when his greatness is recalled. This is the background often combined with Jambavan’s speech in popular storytelling.

The speech itself is in [Kishkindha Kanda 66](/ramayana/kishkindha-kanda#jambavan). Keeping the locations separate allows the later explanation to illuminate the earlier scene without claiming that the earlier scene contains every detail. Our article [Why Did Hanuman Forget His Powers?](/articles/why-hanuman-forgot-his-powers-jambavan-ramayana) examines that connection more closely.

sections.heading: Public suspicion enters the reunited household
paragraphs: Rama honours and dismisses his allies, and the narrative gives a period of happiness with Sita. The interruption comes through reports of what people are saying about her time in Ravana’s captivity. Rama knows the divine affirmation already given in Yuddha Kanda, yet treats public reputation as a demand upon his kingship.

He instructs Lakshmana to leave the pregnant Sita near the hermitages. The journey begins without her knowing its true purpose. Lakshmana’s anguish does not prevent him from carrying out the order, and Sita must respond to a decision made in her absence.

Valmiki receives her and provides protection. The episode should be named plainly as abandonment or exile, rather than softened into a voluntary spiritual retreat. It is also different from the earlier fire ordeal: the latter took place after the war in Lanka; this separation occurs later, during Rama’s reign.

sections.heading: The stories between the great turning points
paragraphs: The book pauses to interpret suffering through older narratives. Sumantra’s account to Lakshmana includes a history involving Bhrigu and Vishnu. Rama then recounts stories associated with rulers and sages, including Nriga, Nimi and Yayati.

These passages consider a ruler’s availability to petitioners, the force of a curse, succession and the consequences of desire. They are part of the book’s interest in kingship, not an unrelated collection placed between the exile of Sita and the appearance of her sons.

Shastri’s supplementary chapters after 59 include further material about royal justice. Because editions organize this material differently, the lettered references matter. Readers comparing versions should compare the event as well as the chapter number.

sections.heading: Shatrughna’s campaign and the birth of Lava and Kusha
paragraphs: Ascetics seek help against Lavana. Shatrughna undertakes the campaign, receiving instructions and the means to confront a dangerous opponent. His journey brings him to Valmiki’s hermitage, where the births of Sita’s twins are placed within the narrative.

The stories of Saudasa and Mandhata contribute histories of royal power and its limits. Shatrughna kills Lavana and establishes his rule in Madhu’s city. When he later returns to the hermitage, the recitation of Rama’s story is already part of its life.

This section gives Shatrughna a sustained role beyond being the brother who remains near Bharata. It also allows Lava and Kusha to grow within the world of the poem before their identity becomes central at Rama’s sacrifice.

sections.heading: Shambuka and the book’s difficult social claims
paragraphs: A brahmin brings his dead son before the king, and the narrative connects the death with a perceived violation of the age’s social and religious order. Rama searches his kingdom, finds Shambuka performing austerities, asks about his status and purpose, and kills him. The child’s restoration is presented as confirming the action within the story’s framework.

That framework has been challenged by many readers and interpreters. Describing it does not require endorsing a hierarchy in which spiritual practice is restricted by birth. The killing and the role of varna in the explanation must remain explicit if the episode is discussed.

The surrounding chapters include Agastya’s stories of Shveta and Danda, again connecting royal conduct, wrongdoing and consequences. The Danda narrative addresses sexual violence and the destruction associated with his act. These passages contribute to the severity of the book’s account of rule.

sections.heading: Why the epic’s singers come before Rama
paragraphs: Rama considers a royal sacrifice. Bharata argues against the Rajasuya, and the discussion turns toward the Ashvamedha. Narratives of Vritra and Ila help explain the rite’s significance within the book before preparations begin.

Valmiki brings Lava and Kusha to recite the Ramayana. The king becomes a listener to the story of his own life. This returns the narrative to the singing introduced in Bala Kanda and places poetry in a position to confront power with memory.

The twins’ performance gradually reveals their connection with Rama. The received account here should not be replaced without attribution by every familiar later story of the boys capturing a sacrificial horse and defeating the royal army. The recital is the crucial event in this sequence.

sections.heading: Sita’s final declaration and return to the Earth
paragraphs: Rama summons Sita, and Valmiki publicly affirms her integrity. She makes a final declaration of fidelity and calls upon the Earth to receive her. The Earth opens, and she departs from the human assembly.

This is not another return to the palace. Rama responds with grief and anger, and Brahma addresses him. The poem leaves the reader with the cost of a demand for proof repeated after proof had already been given.

The account of the queens’ deaths and Rama’s continued rule follows. Public continuity does not cancel private loss. A summary that moves directly from the twins’ recognition to a restored happy family would give the wrong ending to Sita’s story in this book.

sections.heading: Lakshmana and Rama reach the end of their earthly roles
paragraphs: The later chapters arrange kingdoms for the next generation. A visit from Kala, Time or Death, then brings Rama’s own earthly mission toward its end. A condition of privacy creates another conflict of duties when Durvasa arrives and demands an audience.

Lakshmana breaks the condition to avert the threatened consequences for others. Rama must then separate from him in accordance with the binding terms. Lakshmana’s departure is followed by Rama’s decisions for his sons, allies and remaining kingdom.

Rama undertakes the final departure toward the Sarayu, accompanied by many who choose to follow him. The conclusion returns his identity to a divine setting and closes with praise of the Ramayana’s recitation. The seven-book journey has moved from a question about an exemplary person to the life of a story that will continue to be heard.

questions.question: Is Uttara Kanda part of the Valmiki Ramayana?
questions.answer: It is part of the received seven-book text and is included in the Critical Edition. Scholarship also discusses its later development relative to much of the central narrative. Those statements address different questions and can both be true.

questions.question: Is Sita’s exile the same event as the fire ordeal?
questions.answer: No. The fire ordeal occurs in Yuddha Kanda after Ravana’s defeat. Sita’s later exile occurs in Uttara Kanda after Rama has returned to rule Ayodhya.

questions.question: Why do some Uttara Kanda chapter numbers differ?
questions.answer: Editions contain different arrangements and supplementary material. This guide uses Shastri’s main numbering through 111 and explicitly notes his lettered supplementary chapters.
